analysis.one_liner: Doubles the tax on bonuses paid by bailed-out firms the government majority-owns.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; after its March 17, 2009 introduction it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended, and the federal government never collected a penny under it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added an extra tax equal to 100% of any bonus paid by a company that took federal bailout money under TARP and was still majority-owned by the government. In practice, that meant firms like the insurance giant AIG, where taxpayers had put up most of the money and where large bonuses paid in early 2009 had triggered a public backlash. Bonus money taxed away would have gone to the Treasury instead of to executives.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, because a 100% surtax on bonuses at government-majority-owned bailout recipients would route that money back to the Treasury rather than to executives of firms kept alive with public money.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an additional income tax equal to the full amount of any bonus paid by a company that received TARP assistance and in which the federal government owns more than 50% of the stock, profits, or beneficial interests [S3].
Applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2008, so it would have reached the bonuses paid in 2009 at firms the government effectively owned [S3].
Covers controlled groups and their foreign subsidiaries, so a bonus paid through an affiliate could not escape the tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employees of majority-government-owned bailout recipients, mainly executives and traders at firms like AIG, who would have owed a tax equal to their entire bonus.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies only to companies where the government owns a majority stake, so most TARP recipients would have been untouched and their executives' bonuses untaxed [S3].

The tax is triggered by the fact of ownership rather than the size or structure of the bonus, and the 100% rate effectively confiscates the payment, which critics at the time argued was unfair and retroactive punishment aimed at a specific group of workers rather than sound tax policy.
The bill exempts salary and commissions from the definition of bonus, which would have pushed firms to restructure pay into forms the tax does not reach [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real grievance — bonuses at firms surviving on taxpayer money — but only at the handful of companies the government actually majority-owned, leaving most bailout recipients' pay structures alone. Its 100% rate was blunt and its exemptions for salary and commission gave firms an easy path around it. Still, for the firms it did reach, it would have returned bonus money to taxpayers at no cost to the general public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 111th Congress ended without a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on March 17, 2009, with five original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans did [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action, and the bill never received a floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and employees of majority-government-owned bailout recipients kept their bonuses untaxed, and taxpayers recouped nothing through this route.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 17, 2009 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 17, 2009 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors and the sponsor were House Democrats; no House Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in committee without a vote that would have tested support further.

industries.industry: Executives and employees of government-majority-owned bailout recipients
industries.note: The bill would have taxed away 100% of their bonuses at firms like AIG, where the government owned a controlling stake after the 2008 financial crisis rescue. Their gain in keeping the bonuses was the public's loss, since the money came out of firms kept afloat with taxpayer funds.

Only firms majority-owned by the federal government were covered, so the broader industry's bonus practices were untouched. Firms that had repaid TARP aid or kept government ownership below 50% faced no tax.
